In progress 1. "Unseen and Uncounted: How Bureaucracy and Community Organizing Made New Racial Groups in America." (based on [dissertation](https://escholarship.org/content/qt3531f8fr/qt3531f8fr.pdf)) - Interviewed by [Scope Conditions podcast](https://www.scopeconditionspodcast.com/episodes/episode-34-comparing-asian-coalitions-across-three-chinatowns-with-jae-yeon-kim?fbclid=IwAR1_zGE57lmVDhg8uQA8FfDbdzOybB704Q2m0VQkkhfWtB7Asj29I_-mxPM) - Winner of the 2022 Best Dissertation Award, Urban and Local Politics, APSA - Winner of the 2020 Best Paper Award, Asian Pacific American Politics, WPSA - Datasets: [Asian American and Latino Advocacy and Community Service Organizations Dataset (1868-2016)](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/FLUPBJ) - Interactive Map: [Asian American and Latino Advocacy and Community Service Organizations](https://jaeyk.github.io/aa_latino_organizations_map/) **Unseen and Uncounted: How Bureaucracy and Community Organizing Made New Racial Groups in America** introduces the concept of *classification cost* to explain how the administrative challenges of identifying and categorizing marginalized communities shaped the rise of new racial group formations. Identifying diverse target populations through simple administrative categories is not an easy task. These challenges became especially salient during the War on Poverty, when the federal government sought to expand safety net programs without revising how it categorized target populations. When the cost of recognizing small, fragmented, or poorly understood immigrant populations was deemed too high, the state often defaulted to residual labels such as “Other.” Faced with exclusion from official categories, ethnic elites engaged in political innovation. They coined new panethnic labels, built coalitions across national-origin lines, and established civic organizations that rendered their communities legible to the state. These bottom-up efforts reduced classification cost for local government agencies and reshaped how race was codified in public policy. Over time, these strategies scaled upward, influencing federal classification schemes and institutionalizing panethnic categories such as “Asian American” and “Latino.” Drawing on original data from both local administrators and community organizers, the book traces the evolution of policies governing diverse low-income populations at the subnational, national, and transnational levels during the postwar period of American political development. Governing diversity is challenging for both administrative and political reasons, and these challenges are inherently connected. Classifying diverse groups is costly, and unless target groups develop the capacity to make themselves legible, the state has difficulty recognizing them and distributing resources fairly. Sample chapters are available upon request. I plan to complete the first draft by 2026. **Table of Contents** - *Identity Politics is Just Politics* - Chapter 1. War on Poverty, Classification Cost, and Community Organizing - Chapter 2. Visibility Is the Name of the Game: Organizational Adaptation Under the War on Poverty - Chapter 3. A Tale of Three Chinatowns: Political Geography, Trust, and Paths to Solidarity - Chapter 4. Unwinding: How Class and Race Fall Out of Alignment - Chapter 5. Classification Cost and New Group Formation: The Cases of Disability and Gig Worker Rights - *Governing Diversity: Why Both State and Civic Capacity Matter* **Pictures from the archives and field** ![Enter Opportunity Market. Source: Agenda, the newsletter of the National Council of La Raza Fall 1974 (p.20)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jaeyk/jaeyk.github.io/main/misc/garcia.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"} ![The Unity Council (est in 1964, Fruitvale, Oakland, CA). Photo Credit: Jae Yeon Kim (2025)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jaeyk/jaeyk.github.io/main/misc/unity_council.JPG){fig-align="center" width="60%"} *Note: [The Unity Council](https://unitycouncil.org/about-us/) was "the first Spanish-language focused employment center in Oakland and served as an anchor response to President Lyndon B. Johnson’s War on Poverty."* ![Chinese for Affirmative Action (est in 1969. Chinatown, San Francisco, CA). Photo Credit: Jae Yeon Kim (2025)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jaeyk/jaeyk.github.io/main/misc/caa.png){fig-align="center" width="60%"} *Note: [Chinese for Affirmative Action](https://caasf.org/mission-vision-history/) was established to leverage War on Poverty resources and to advocate for fair education and employment opportunities for Chinatown residents.*
Books 2. ["We Need Civic Data: How Public Data Can Fail Us, and How It Can Build a More Just Society (in Korean)."](http://www.sejongbooks.co.kr/?act=board.index&bbs_code=sub2_1&sc=bbs_title&ss=%EC%9A%B0%EB%A6%AC%EC%97%90%EA%B2%8C%EB%8A%94&page=1&bbs_mode=view&bbs_seq=160) (in Korean, Sejong Books 2023) \[[book website](https://wethedata.vercel.app/)\] Why can we shop with one click but still struggle to access basic public services? *We Need Civic Data* is the first book in Korean to comprehensively examine the concept, practice, and promise of civic data, data designed not for profit or bureaucratic procedure, but for the public good. Written by social data scientist and public interest technologist Jae Yeon Kim, the book draws on real-world policy examples from the U.S. and South Korea to show how government data systems shape who gets access to benefits, who gets heard, and who gets left behind. Across ten clear and accessible chapters, Kim offers a roadmap for building a more equitable, human-centered digital state. **Impact & Recognition** - Selected as one of **70 finalists by the Korean Government** in the popular social science category for 2024; the government purchased approximately **500 copies** and distributed them to public libraries nationwide - Recommended by [the *National Assembly Library*](https://shorturl.at/7Oc1Z), *Samsung Global Research*'s executive education program (*SERICEO*), and [the *Korea Institute of Science and Technology* (KIST)](https://library.kist.re.kr/search/recommend.do) - Featured in major Korean newspapers across the ideological spectrum: [*The Chosun Ilbo*](https://futurechosun.com/archives/80334), [*Maeil Business Newspaper*](https://www.mk.co.kr/news/culture/10825533), [*The Korea Economic Daily*](https://www.hankyung.com/article/202309136820i), [*Kyunghyang Shinmun*](https://www.khan.co.kr/culture/book/article/202309082034005), [*Hankyoreh*](https://h21.hani.co.kr/arti/world/world_general/54378.html) - Regular op-eds based on the book published in: [*Chosun Ilbo*'s Civic Section](https://www.futurechosun.com/archives/96581?fbclid=IwY2xjawErhE9leHRuA2FlbQIxMAABHd-SqBkJfRkTibVjqv7FG5oTLHeR0ZMNh4mGqQC4ORkSWD4JQz-1MoMtew_aem_uB833DJQzDbI5078qlr8eA) *(a major conservative newspaper)* and [*Weekly Kyunghang*](https://weekly.khan.co.kr/khnm.html?mode=list&s_code=ne039) *(a major liberal magazine)* ::: center ![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jaeyk/jaeyk.github.io/main/misc/civic_data_book.jpg){fig-align="center"} 1. ["How to Use University: Learning How to Learn and Why It Matters for a Fulfilling Career (in Korean)"](https://www.yes24.com/product/goods/183755163) (Sejong Books, 2nd ed., 2026) [[book website](https://learn2career.vercel.app/)] Why do so many students enter college full of ambition, only to graduate with more confusion than clarity? *How to Use University* is a practical guide to navigating college with purpose. Organized around four core themes, exploring college, learning, career, and life, it helps students shift from passive schooling to intentional, opportunity-driven learning. The book encourages students to treat the university as a **launchpad** for discovering interests, initiating projects, and building community. It emphasizes a key idea: unlocking even one small opportunity, especially a self-initiated project, can set off a **cycle of opportunities** that grows over time. **Impact & Recognition** - The first edition sold over **10,000 copies** and has been widely recommended by educators, university counselors, and mentoring programs across South Korea - Featured in major Korean media outlets including *Maeil Business Newspaper* and *Chosun Biz* - Frequently used in student development seminars and campus book clubs - A fully revised **second edition was published in 2026.**

document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', function() {
  var searchInput = document.querySelector('#quarto-search input[type="text"], .aa-Input');
  if (searchInput) {
    searchInput.setAttribute('placeholder', 'Search this site...');
  }

  // Auto-size reversed list numbering from actual item count.
  document.querySelectorAll('.reversed-list > ol').forEach(function(ol) {
    var wrapper = ol.closest('.reversed-list');
    if (!wrapper) return;

    // Allow manual override via --reversed-counter-reset when needed.
    var manualReset = wrapper.style.getPropertyValue('--reversed-counter-reset');
    if (manualReset && manualReset.trim() !== '') return;

    var itemCount = Array.from(ol.children).filter(function(child) {
      return child.tagName === 'LI';
    }).length;

    wrapper.style.setProperty('--reversed-counter-reset', String(itemCount + 1));
  });
});
</script>
